text:
GET /index.html 200
POST /api/login 401
GET /api/users 200
GET /missing 404
POST /api/login 200
DELETE /api/users/7 403
GET /index.html 200
PUT /api/users/3 200
GET /api/orders 500
description: Count the requests per HTTP method (1st field) with a single awk and print "METHOD COUNT", sorted by method name.
solution: awk '{count[$1]++} END {for (m in count) print m, count[m]}' | sort
hint: Use: awk '{count[$1]++} END {for (m in count) print m, count[m]}' | sort - an array counts per key; "for (k in arr)" has no fixed order, so sort afterwards

text:
books,12.50
games,59.99
books,7.25
music,9.99
games,19.99
books,30.00
music,14.50
description: Sum the amounts (2nd field) per category (1st field) and print "category total", sorted by category.
solution: awk -F',' '{sum[$1] += $2} END {for (c in sum) print c, sum[c]}' | sort
hint: Use: awk -F',' '{sum[$1] += $2} END {for (c in sum) print c, sum[c]}' | sort - sum[key] += value accumulates per key

text:
books,12.50
games,59.99
books,7.25
music,9.99
games,19.99
books,30.00
music,14.50
description: Print a table: the category left-aligned in 8 characters, then the amount right-aligned in 7 characters with 2 decimals (e.g. "books      12.50").
expected:
books     12.50
games     59.99
books      7.25
music      9.99
games     19.99
books     30.00
music     14.50
hint: Use: awk -F',' '{printf "%-8s%7.2f\n", $1, $2}' - %-8s pads a string on the right, %7.2f is a number 7 wide with 2 decimals; printf adds no newline by itself

text:

description: Print every student followed by "pass" if the score is 60 or more, otherwise "fail".
expected:
alice pass
bob fail
carol pass
dave fail
eve pass
frank pass
hint: Use: awk '{if ($2 >= 60) print $1, "pass"; else print $1, "fail"}' - if/else works like in C

description: Print the student with the highest score as "name score" — in one awk, without sort.
solution: awk 'NR == 1 || $2 > max {max = $2; name = $1} END {print name, max}'
hint: Use: awk 'NR == 1 || $2 > max {max = $2; name = $1} END {print name, max}' - remember the best value seen so far

text:
alice 82
bob 47
carol 95
dave 59
eve 60
frank 71
description: Print the average score with exactly 2 decimals.
hint: Use: awk '{sum += $2} END {printf "%.2f\n", sum / NR}' - NR in END is the number of lines

text:
banana
apple
banana
cherry
apple
date
banana
description: Remove duplicate lines but keep the original order (the first occurrence of each line) — sort -u would change the order.
hint: Use: awk '!seen[$0]++' - the pattern is true only the first time a line is seen

text:
alice admin
bob dev
carol ops
dave dev
description: Print every user name in UPPERCASE followed by the length of the name.
hint: Use: awk '{print toupper($1), length($1)}' - toupper() and length() are built-in functions

text:
January 31
February 28
March 31
April 30
May 31
description: Print only the first 3 letters of every month name.
hint: Use: awk '{print substr($1, 1, 3)}' - substr(string, start, length), positions start at 1

text:
2024-01-15 deploy
2024-02-03 rollback
2024-02-20 deploy
description: Replace every "-" in the lines with "/" using awk (e.g. "2024/01/15 deploy").
hint: Use: awk '{gsub(/-/, "/"); print}' - gsub replaces all matches in $0 (sub replaces only the first)

text:
report.pdf 120
photo.jpg 2048
notes.txt 3
video.mp4 90000
song.mp3 5120
description: Pass the limit as a variable: print files whose size (2nd field) is at least 1000, using awk -v limit=1000.
hint: Use: awk -v limit=1000 '$2 >= limit' - -v sets a variable before the program runs

text:
alice 30 kyiv
bob 25 lviv
carol 41 odesa
description: Convert the space-separated lines to CSV (commas between fields) with awk.
hint: Use: awk -v OFS=',' '{$1 = $1; print}' - assigning a field rebuilds the line with the output separator OFS

text:
header

footer
description: Print everything from the "# BEGIN CONFIG" line to the "# END CONFIG" line (both included).
expected:
# BEGIN CONFIG
port=8080
host=example.com
# END CONFIG
hint: Use: awk '/BEGIN CONFIG/,/END CONFIG/' - a range pattern "start, end" selects the lines in between

text:
backup.tar.gz
report.pdf
photo.jpeg
archive.tar.bz2
README
description: Print the last extension of every file name (the text after the last dot); names without a dot print the whole name.
hint: Use: awk -F'.' '{print $NF}' - with "." as separator the last field is the extension

hint: Use: sort -hr | head -3 - -h understands K, M, G suffixes; plain -n would think 900K > 2.5G

description: Print the newest version (versions compare number by number: 1.10 is newer than 1.9).
hint: Use: sort -V | tail -1 - version sort compares the numbers inside the strings

text: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog and keeps running far away

The quick brown fox 
jumps over the lazy 
dog and keeps

hint: Use: fold -s -w 20 - -w sets the width, -s breaks at spaces instead of in the middle of words

description: Print the numbers from 1 to 10 on one line, separated by commas. (There is no input text: generate the numbers.)
hint: Use: seq -s, 10 - seq prints number sequences, -s sets the separator

description: Print "item-01" to "item-05", one per line.
hint: Use: seq -f 'item-%02g' 5 - -f uses a printf format; %02g pads with zeros (seq 5 | awk '{printf "item-%02d\n", $1}' works too)

description: Swap commas and semicolons in one step: every "," becomes ";" and every ";" becomes ",".
hint: Use: sed 'y/,;/;,/' - y/abc/xyz/ translates characters one to one (like tr)

hint: Use: sed '1i name,score' - "i" inserts a line before the addressed one ("a" appends after it)

hint: Use: sed '2,3c [secrets removed]' - "c" changes the addressed lines; for a range the text replaces the whole range once

description: Using an awk function: define function isup(s) that returns 1 when s is "up", and print the interfaces that are up.
hint: Use: awk 'function isup(s) {return s == "up"} isup($2) {print $1}' - functions are defined outside of the { } rules

description: For every status code print how many requests got it and which paths (in input order, separated by spaces), e.g. "200 5: /index.html ...", sorted by status code.
solution: awk '{n[$3]++; paths[$3] = paths[$3] " " $2} END {for (s in n) print s, n[s] ":" paths[s]}' | sort
hint: Use: awk '{n[$3]++; paths[$3] = paths[$3] " " $2} END {for (s in n) print s, n[s] ":" paths[s]}' | sort - two arrays with the same keys; strings are joined by writing them next to each other
